vid-b1-what-ai-video-can-do-first-clip.q: A colleague on the free Gemini app plan wants to start generating Veo clips today. What should you tell them?
options: Veo access requires at least a Google AI Pro (~$19.99/mo) plan — the Gemini free tier doesn't include meaningful Veo access
The free tier includes unlimited Veo generations
Veo only works through a separate app, never through Gemini
Free tier users get Veo access but only in black and white
vid-b1-what-ai-video-can-do-first-clip.why: Veo has no meaningful free tier — it's accessed through a Google AI Pro or Ultra plan inside the Gemini app, which is worth knowing before budgeting a video project.

vid-b1-what-ai-video-can-do-first-clip.q: A colleague wants one prompt to generate a full 3-scene story with dialogue in a single Veo generation. Is this realistic today?
options: Yes, one generation reliably creates a full multi-shot sequence with dialogue
No — one generation is one short clip (typically 5-8 seconds), not a multi-shot story; plan per-shot and use scene extension for longer sequences
Only through Google AI Studio, never the Gemini app
Yes, as long as the prompt is written long enough
vid-b1-what-ai-video-can-do-first-clip.why: Veo reliably produces one short clip per generation; a multi-scene story requires planning individual shots and stitching or extending them, not one giant prompt.

vid-b1-what-ai-video-can-do-first-clip.q: You write a prompt for your first Veo clip but leave out any description of sound. What actually happens?
options: Veo generates the clip completely silent, with no audio track at all
Veo pauses generation and asks you to add a sound description first
Veo generates synchronized audio anyway, since it produces sound natively — leaving the cue unstated just means you didn't control what it is
Sound can only be added afterward in a separate app; Veo never generates audio
vid-b1-what-ai-video-can-do-first-clip.why: Veo generates synchronized audio as part of every clip. If you don't describe the sound you want, Veo still produces something — so an unstated sound cue is a missed control, not a way to get silence.

vid-b2-motion-first-prompts.q: A prompt describes "she stands up, walks to the door, opens it" as the action for one 5-second clip. What's the problem?
options: That's ideal, since it packs more story into the clip
This works fine, as long as the camera line is also detailed
Sequential actions actually improve prompt adherence in Veo
A 5-8 second clip can't reliably show three sequential beats — the action should be described as one continuous motion
vid-b2-motion-first-prompts.why: A short clip can't cleanly render three distinct sequential events; describing one continuous motion is what Veo can actually follow within that duration.

vid-b2-motion-first-prompts.q: Why does the lesson add "Sound" as one of the six prompt elements, alongside subject, action, camera, setting/lighting, and style?
options: Because Veo generates synchronized audio natively, so describing sound is part of controlling the shot, not an optional extra
Because sound only matters for dialogue-heavy clips
Because it's required by the Gemini app's upload form
Because it replaces the need to describe camera movement
vid-b2-motion-first-prompts.why: Veo produces audio together with the video by default, so leaving sound undescribed still results in an audio track — just one you didn't control. Naming it deliberately is how you take charge of that element too.

vid-b2-motion-first-prompts.q: You leave the camera movement unstated in your prompt. What should you expect?
options: Veo always pauses and asks you to clarify the camera move first
Leaving camera movement unstated leads to generic default motion, since Veo defaults to something if you don't specify
Unspecified camera always defaults to a dramatic orbit shot
It has no effect on the resulting clip
vid-b2-motion-first-prompts.why: Veo falls back to a default — often static or a generic push — when camera movement isn't named explicitly, so being explicit is how you actually take control of the shot.

vid-i1-storyboard-prompts.q: ChatGPT hands you a 4-shot list for your concept. What should you do with it next?
options: Paste each shot description straight into Veo exactly as ChatGPT wrote it
Rewrite each beat into a proper motion-first Veo prompt with camera, sound, and a shared continuity block — ChatGPT's list is a planning draft, not a finished prompt
Discard it, since ChatGPT can't be used for planning video content
Only use it to pick a title for the finished video
vid-i1-storyboard-prompts.why: ChatGPT is useful for structuring the beats, but it doesn't know Veo's prompt conventions — each shot still needs to be rewritten as a proper motion-first prompt with a shared continuity block before generating.

vid-i1-storyboard-prompts.q: What is the continuity block's primary purpose in a multi-shot Veo sequence?
options: To decorate the prompt with extra adjectives
To satisfy a required minimum prompt length
To specify only camera angles for each shot
A reusable phrase describing the subject's appearance, environment, and style, pasted identically into every shot's prompt to prevent drift
vid-i1-storyboard-prompts.why: Pasting an identical continuity block into every shot is what stops Veo from quietly re-imagining the subject or setting between separate generations.

vid-i1-storyboard-prompts.q: In your shot list, you call the mug "a red mug" in shot 1 and "a ceramic cup" in shot 3. What happens?
options: No issue — Veo recognizes synonyms perfectly across shots
This actually improves visual variety intentionally
This reads to Veo as a different element, causing continuity drift — reuse the exact same wording for the same element across shots
It only affects the audio, not the object's appearance
vid-i1-storyboard-prompts.why: Different wording for the same recurring element is interpreted by Veo as a genuinely different object, which is exactly how continuity drifts between shots.

vid-i2-product-promo-clips-social.q: You need a promo clip where the product's exact label and logo stay accurate. What approach should you use?
options: Text-to-video, describing the product's appearance in exhaustive detail
Image-to-video from a real product photo, since text-to-video risks Veo reinventing label text or the logo
Ask Veo to render the logo carefully within a text prompt
Use a generic stock photo of a similar product instead
vid-i2-product-promo-clips-social.why: Animating a real product photo with Veo's image-to-video keeps packaging, logo, and color accurate, sidestepping text-to-video's known unreliability at rendering exact text and logos.

vid-i2-product-promo-clips-social.q: When animating a real product photo, why should the prompt describe only motion and sound, not the product's appearance?
options: Because appearance descriptions are ignored by image-to-video anyway
Because it saves characters in the prompt, nothing more
Because the source photo already defines the product's appearance — describing it again invites Veo to reinvent details like label text
Because appearance and motion can never both be described in one prompt
vid-i2-product-promo-clips-social.why: The photo already fixes what the product looks like; re-describing it in text gives Veo an opening to change details like label wording that should stay untouched.

vid-i2-product-promo-clips-social.q: You want a clean product clip with no music, just quiet ambient sound. What should you do?
options: Leave the sound cue out of the prompt entirely, since silence is the default
State it explicitly, e.g. "ambient room tone only, no music" — Veo generates audio either way, so an unstated cue risks an unwanted soundtrack
Add the phrase "no audio" and expect a fully silent file
Sound can only be controlled after generation, in the editor
vid-i2-product-promo-clips-social.why: Since Veo produces synchronized audio natively, getting the clean, quiet track you want means stating that intent directly in the prompt, not assuming silence is the default.

vid-i3-iterate-extend-retime-fix.q: A clip is good overall but has one glitchy hand at second 3. What's the most efficient fix?
options: Regenerate with a small, targeted addition naming the exact fix (e.g., "keep hands out of frame"), leaving the rest of the prompt unchanged
Rewrite the entire prompt from scratch
Use scene extension to try to move past the glitch
Switch to describing the scene in a completely different way
vid-i3-iterate-extend-retime-fix.why: A targeted fix changes as little as possible on top of a prompt that was already mostly working, preserving everything correct while addressing only the specific flaw.

vid-i3-iterate-extend-retime-fix.q: Why should a Veo extension prompt avoid re-describing the whole scene, including the sound?
options: Re-describing the scene is actually required for extensions to work correctly
Re-describing the scene and sound risks Veo treating it as a new, disconnected shot instead of continuing from the last frame with matching audio
It has no real effect on continuity either way
Sound is never generated during scene extension, so it doesn't matter
vid-i3-iterate-extend-retime-fix.why: Scene extension continues from the clip's final frame and audio automatically; re-describing the whole scene is exactly what causes Veo to treat it as a fresh, unrelated generation instead.

vid-i3-iterate-extend-retime-fix.q: A generated take is fundamentally wrong in composition and mood, not just one detail off. What should you do?
options: Never — always patch, regardless of how wrong the take is
Only regenerate fully when the clip's duration is too short
When the take is fundamentally wrong in composition, mood, or subject placement — patching a bad take usually costs more attempts than starting over
Whenever any hand glitch appears, however minor
vid-i3-iterate-extend-retime-fix.why: Patching is reserved for a mostly-working shot with one flaw; a fundamentally wrong take is cheaper to fix by regenerating from a revised prompt than by trying to patch it repeatedly.

vid-a1-production-workflow.q: A creator generates three great individual Veo clips and publishes them stitched together with no editing pass. What's likely to happen?
options: This is fine, since Veo clips already look polished on their own
Editing is optional specifically for social platforms
Editing only matters for videos over 60 seconds long
Skipping editing usually reads as unpolished even when individual clips look great — cuts, text, a clean audio mix, and a hook/CTA are what make it finished content
vid-a1-production-workflow.why: Veo generates footage and audio, it doesn't finish a piece of content — the edit pass (trimming, audio mix, text, hook, CTA) is what turns raw clips into something that reads as produced content.

vid-a1-production-workflow.q: Why does the lesson recommend adding on-screen marketing text and captions in the video editor rather than relying on Veo?
options: Editors render exact text reliably, while Veo doesn't reliably render exact on-screen text or logos
Veo is technically incapable of ever generating any audio
It's simply cheaper to add text inside Veo
Captions must legally be added only in post-production
vid-a1-production-workflow.why: Veo is known to be unreliable at rendering exact text, while a standard editor renders typed text reliably, so final marketing copy and captions belong in the edit.

vid-a1-production-workflow.q: Before publishing, you paste your edit description into Claude with a review prompt that restricts it to only the pacing, hook, and cut details you've described. Why restrict it that way?
options: It's a formality that has no real function in the review
Restricting the review to only what you've described produces a grounded critique on pacing, hook, and CTA instead of generic advice or invented assumptions
It replaces the need to actually watch the final export before publishing
It guarantees the finished video will perform well
vid-a1-production-workflow.why: Feeding the reviewer only the facts you supply keeps its critique grounded in your actual edit rather than generic advice based on assumptions about details you never gave it.
